response.text:
I need to be careful here. The finding is a closed-period posting: journal 2463 was posted to period 7 (closed) after its close date. The fix convention says a correction must go into an open period, and the journal itself is not edited. Reversing 2463 and re-posting in an open period would be the typical correction, but the finding is about the posting itself, and the convention allows a correcting journal that references the original.

The journal 2463 balances: DR 5382.28 vs CR 2691.14 + 2691.14 = 5382.28. Good.

A proper correction: reverse the original in an open period (period 11 or 12) with lines mirroring the original with DR/CR swapped, referencing corrects_jrnl_no 2463. That nets the original to zero. Re-posting the entry in an open period is a separate decision that I shouldn't assume; the reversal alone removes the closed-period effect from the ledger balances as presented, but it also means the expense is not recognized anywhere. Since the finding is only that the posting was made after close, the minimal fix that leaves the business entry intact is to reverse in period 7's successor... but period 7 is closed, so I must use an open period. The cleanest reversal-and-repost would net to the original amounts in the open period, which is effectively moving the entry to period 11. I'll do that: a reversal in period 11 plus a repost in period 11, which nets the original to zero and places the same amounts in an open period. That is two-sided per line-set and balances.

Net effect of the group (original + correction) needs to match the right position. Moving the entry to period 11 means the correction lines are: reverse (CR 5100 5382.28; DR 2100 2691.14; DR 1200 2691.14) plus repost (DR 5100 5382.28; CR 2100 2691.14; CR 1200 2691.14). Those net to zero in each account, so the group balances and the original amounts are retained in an open period only if the repost is counted as the true position. Since the reversal and repost in the same journal cancel out completely, the net effect in the ledger is nothing, which does not move the entry. That makes this an unsound construction.

A correct minimal approach: the only way to move an amount from a closed period to an open one is a reversal in the closed period (not allowed) or a reversal in an open period plus a repost in an open period. Doing both in the same journal nets to zero, so it does not change balances. The honest answer is that the finding cannot be fixed by a balance-changing correction within the convention without a business decision about whether the accrual should be reversed or kept. I should not invent one.

Given that, I'll submit a reversal of 2463 in open period 11 with no repost, which removes the unauthorized closed-period accrual from the ledger, and flag that the entry should be re-booked by the controller if it is valid.

arguments.reasoning: Journal 2463 (manual GL accrual, memo 'Manual accrual', SRC_REF JSMITH) was posted to period 7 on 20240808, after that period closed on 20240805, so it cannot be edited or re-dated. The correction reverses its effect in open period 11 (the only open periods are 11 and 12), referencing 2463 via corrects_jrnl_no. Lines swap the original DR/CR: CR 5100 5382.28, DR 2100 2691.14, DR 1200 2691.14. The group (original plus correction) balances and nets the 2463 accounts to zero. Caveat: this reversal removes the accrual from the ledger entirely; if the accrual is valid it must be re-booked by an authorized user in an open period, which I have not done because it is a business decision. No invoice status changes, since this is not a duplicate-invoice finding. Note that journal 2462 (period 4) has the same closed-period issue and is not covered by this finding (F002-2 covers 2463 only).
